groups.title: Persian sayings
groups.q: Some Persian sayings and images are translated word for word. Does each one give you some sense of its meaning, or does it mean nothing to you?
groups.note_label: What do you think it means?

rows.text: Rain doesn't fall upward from the earth.
A good year is known from its spring.
Don't eat sorrow
my heart is rotting
My hand is short and union with you is far.
if I say it, my tongue burns; if I don't say it, the marrow of my bones burns
the meal will turn to snake venom for me
no bread is going to warm up for you
my family shoved me into the henhouse
the sugar cube jumps in my throat
peek into every last corner
words cost nothing; it's just hot air
he would surely fall from Negar's eyes
Just a harvest-time promise?
let me serve you the guts of friendship on a tray
all their body hair fell right out
don't get so worked up, or your milk will dry up
no one will call you mute if you don't fart
Eat the head of my dick
You dick-head eater
laughing at our beards and dicks
wandering the streets like this with your dick in your hand
no matter what dick lands on our heads

groups.title: Children's words
groups.q: Some children in the book get words wrong, the way small children do. Does each one sound like a child's mistake, not a typo?

rows.text: It's marmal stone. Marmal means really expensive.
rows.note: marmal = marble

rows.text: It's called Tatanic.
rows.note: Tatanic = Titanic

rows.text: Baba, Baba, wiw you buy me dis big dolly?
rows.note: a little girl

rows.text: Yes, I wiw buy you a dolly.
rows.note: her father copies her

groups.title: Nicknames
groups.q: The friends in the book give each other playful nicknames, often as wordplay. Does each one work as a nickname in your language?

rows.text: Alain Dickon
rows.note: a nickname for one of the friends: the actor Alain Delon's name, with part of it turned into a rude word for penis

rows.text: Elder of the Tavern
rows.note: a mock-grand title, taken from Hafez's poetry

rows.text: Eldie
rows.note: a pet form of "Elder of the Tavern"

rows.text: Taverny, my Tavvy
rows.note: pet forms made from "tavern"

rows.text: Leopard Farid
rows.note: for a daring, reckless friend

rows.text: Is Arasteh a trimmed-down Araasteh?
rows.note: araasteh = Persian for "neat"

rows.text: Her Ladyship Ms. Armaaan
rows.note: the surname Arman, drawn out to mock

rows.text: Mister Curly-haired Schrödinger
rows.note: a mock title for someone who can't make up his mind

groups.title: Jokes and wordplay
groups.q: These lines contain a joke or a play on words. Does each one work in your language?

rows.text: That's just his factory setting.
rows.note: messing things up is simply his nature

rows.text: Forgiven. The whole boulevard is yours.
rows.note: in Persian, "forgive" also means "give away"

rows.text: until yesterday you said "ass." Now you've gone all civilized and say "donkey"?
rows.note: teasing a boy for switching to a politer word

rows.text: Pir-to-pir? … Eagle Eye says peer-to-peer; Taverny says Eldie-to-Eldie.
rows.note: he hears "peer" as Persian pir, "elder", the root of his nickname

rows.text: Last night I could hear you ruminating.
rows.note: chewing at night, like a cow chewing cud

rows.text: What the hell's wrong with you this time, getting it up at us, Alain Dickon?
rows.note: double meaning: sitting up proudly, and an erection

rows.text: What izer wasn't he?
rows.note: the mother catches only the end of "womanizer"

rows.text: The friend of the cousin of our brother-in-law's master craftsman who is the richest man in Tehran
rows.note: a boy's running boast

rows.text: Or you're dick-brai... well, you already were dick-brained, now you've become even more dick-brained.
rows.note: the insult is cut off, then made worse

rows.text: Yeah, all of us own factories. … We've got a bullshit factory.
rows.note: all they produce is bullshit: they just talk nonsense

rows.text: You fossil, you're a monument to stupidity and decline
rows.note: a mocking insult

rows.text: life is like a thousand-toman banknote: whichever side you look at, it smells of lentil rice.
rows.note: an absurd quip

rows.text: This is how I talk; you hear me speak, you think it's poetry.
rows.note: a boy answers in a sing-song rhythm

rows.text: Careful you don't crack, Mr. Dick.
rows.note: he has just puffed out his chest

rows.text: You're the biggest cow of all.
rows.note: "cow" = a dull fool, said to a man

rows.text: he always got such a kick out of working the word "aware" into that sentence twice.
rows.note: "aware" used twice, playfully

rows.text: the problem is with the receiver; the transmitter can't fix it.
rows.note: the friend's poor eyesight is the "receiver"

rows.text: I mean Alain Dickon. Diiick.
rows.note: the rude part of the pun, drawn out

rows.text: If you're Hooman, then I'm Susan.
rows.note: the gentle name Hooman doesn't suit such a hairy man

rows.text: The derivative? Meaning? Or the meaning of the derivative? Or the derivative of meaning?
rows.note: mock-profound wordplay

rows.text: God willing, may you always be araasteh.
rows.note: a blessing that puns on the surname Arasteh; araasteh = "neat"

rows.text: I can't see anything without my glasses, objectively.
rows.note: the character's habit word, used everywhere

groups.title: A line by Hafez
groups.q: This line by the poet Hafez is written without a comma, so it can be read in two opposite ways:

rows.text: The wine there is real no metaphor.

after: One way: the wine is real, not a metaphor.
The other way: the wine is not real, only a metaphor.
groups.after_q: Can your version be read both ways?
